Observed economics show much faster value compression: on-demand rental fell ~64-83% (peak >$8-12/hr in 2023 to ~$2-4/hr by late 2025/2026) within ~18-24 months, and secondary unit prices are off ~30-40% from new with a documented inflection after ~24 months as Blackwell ramps. economic_vs_book_life_note: Hyperscalers/neoclouds depreciate AI servers straight-line over 5-7 years (Amazon explicitly 5yr effective Jan 1 2025, down from 6yr; the 10-K cites 'increased pace of technology development, particularly in AI/ML' as the reason). Observed H200 economics imply a far shorter ECONOMIC life: on-demand rental revenue per GPU-hour has fallen roughly 55-60% from launch-era hyperscaler rates (~$10.60/hr Azure/GCP late-2024) to a ~$4.26/hr market median by June 2026 — within ~18 months — and market trackers project the asset retains only ~25% of purchase value after 3 years (an H100-pattern proxy, since H200 secondary volume barely exists yet). A 5-7yr straight-line book life assumes ~14-20% annual value/earning-power decay; the observed rental-yield compression (~40%/yr) and projected ~75% value loss over 3yr (~25-35%/yr) materially outrun book depreciation, supporting a book-vs-economic-life gap. Caveat: rental rates conflate supply-glut/Blackwell-rotation effects with true obsolescence, and resale figures are projections, not realized H200 trades — so the gap is directional/defensible rather than precisely measured.

economic_vs_book_life_note: The market evidence does NOT show the rapid economic depreciation a naive book-vs-economic thesis would predict for a 2024-launched chip. As of mid-2026 (~2 years post-launch), B200 secondary/OEM unit prices (~$40-50k) sit AT OR ABOVE the ~$30-40k launch range, and on-demand rental rates have been RISING, not falling: Silicon Data's index ran from ~$4.40/hr (Jan 1, 2026) to a $6.11/hr peak (Mar 25, 2026), and the Ornn spot index rose 114% in six weeks to ~$4.95/hr (late Apr 2026), driven by GPT-5.x-class demand outstripping constrained Blackwell supply. So the headline 'decline %' for B200 is currently negative-decline (appreciation) over the periods I could source; the only sustained DECLINE observed is the short intra-month pullback (March 25 peak $6.11 -> March 30 $5.48, -10.3%). The defensible book-vs-economic-life gap therefore does NOT come from B200 prices collapsing under a 5-7yr straight-line book life; it comes from the OPPOSITE direction confirmed in an SEC filing: Amazon (10-Q, effective Jan 1 2025) SHORTENED server/networking useful life from 6yr to 5yr 'due to the increased pace of technology development, particularly in the area of artificial intelligence and machine learning,' adding $889M depreciation / -$677M net income over 9M-2025 (primarily AWS). That hyperscaler accounting shortening (toward, not away from, faster economic obsolescence) is the credible signal that 5-7yr book life understates the speed of generational AI-hardware turnover, even while current-generation Blackwell resale/rental remains strong on supply scarcity. Net: book life 5-7yr; observed B200 economic value over its first ~2yrs has NOT compressed (supply-constrained), but the marginal SEC-disclosed policy move is to shorten lives, implying economic life < legacy 6yr book life for the broader server fleet.

economic_vs_book_life_note: Observed A100 RENTAL economics compress faster than a flat 5-7yr straight-line book line: AWS p4d list was $32.77/hr for 8x A100 (~$4.10/GPU-hr) at Nov-2020 launch vs open-market on-demand A100-80GB now ~$1.6/hr median (floor <$0.80/hr), a ~55-80% per-GPU-hour decline in ~5.5yrs — i.e., unit cash yield is eroding meaningfully before the asset is fully book-depreciated. Hyperscaler book policy is moving the OTHER way to recognize this: Amazon CUT server life 6yr->5yr effective Jan-1-2025 (SEC 10-Q) explicitly citing AI/ML pace, while CoreWeave/neoclouds still depreciate over ~6yr. Crucially, secondary HARDWARE value is sticky (A100-80GB PCIe still ~$18.9k early-2026, ~60-80% retention), so the book-vs-economic gap is driven by collapsing rental/utilization margins, not scrap value — the card stays physically useful (supporting longer book lives) even as its revenue-generating economic life shortens. This is a margin/cash-yield gap rather than an impairment-to-zero gap.

Observed compression points to a much shorter ECONOMIC life: the H800 was discontinued by NVIDIA in 2024 (~1-2 years after launch), removing it from primary supply and leaving little/no liquid secondary or cloud market. China street price fell from a 2023 supply-panic peak of ~$70,000 (and a ~$30,603 US list) to roughly $10,000-15,000/card in 2024 (~60-83% off peak). H800 lacks a continuously tracked $/hr feed; the best live-tracked Hopper analog (H100) shows on-demand rental collapsing ~70% from >$8/hr peak to ~$2.10/hr (Silicon Data index, Dec 17 2025), with renters effectively paying only OpEx-plus-thin-margin per the Princeton CITP analysis. A 60-83% asset price drop and ~70% rental collapse within ~2-3 years are inconsistent with a 5-6yr straight-line book life that retains ~50-67% of cost at year 3, implying hyperscaler/neocloud GPU depreciation schedules materially overstate residual economic value.
